t: Distribute Elements Into Two Arrays II — Editorial
o:
We simulate distributing nums into arr1 and arr2 one element at a time, always needing greaterCount(arr, val): how many elements already in arr are strictly greater than val. The distribution rule only depends on comparing these two counts (with length/tie-breaking), so the whole problem reduces to supporting two operations efficiently: query 'count of elements > val' in a growing multiset, and insert a new element.

Walking through Example 2 ([5,14,3,1,2]): after seeding arr1=[5], arr2=[14], for 3 both counts are 1 and lengths tie, so it goes to arr1; for 1, arr1 has {5,3} both > 1 while arr2 has {14}, so 2>1 and it goes to arr1; similarly 2 goes to arr1, giving result [5,3,1,2,14].

With n up to 10^5, an O(n^2) brute force that scans arrays on each query is borderline-to-too-slow in Python but fine in fast languages; the intended solution uses a Fenwick tree (BIT) over compressed values to answer each count in O(log n). Since we never need order within arr1/arr2 beyond counts, we can just track sizes and use BITs as multisets.
k: The simulation rule only needs greaterCount comparisons plus array lengths — actual element order inside arr1/arr2 is irrelevant.
greaterCount(arr, v) = (size of arr) - (number of elements <= v), so any structure supporting rank queries works.
Coordinate compression + two Fenwick trees gives O(log n) per insert/query, i.e., O(n log n) total.

a.i: Directly maintain arr1 and arr2 as lists and compute greaterCount by linear scan each time. This matches the statement literally and passes in C++/Java/JS given n ≤ 10^5 (about 10^10 worst case? No — each scan is at most current length, so total ~ n^2/2 = 5·10^9... actually queries sum to at most n^2/2 which is too slow in Python but this is the intuitive baseline; still, since each element is scanned once per later query, total work is O(n^2) ≈ 5·10^9 in the worst case, so prefer Approach 2 for safety). We present it as the conceptual baseline.
s: For each subsequent nums[i], compute c1 = number of elements in arr1 greater than nums[i] by scanning, likewise c2.
If c1 > c2 append to arr1; if c1 < c2 append to arr2.
On ties, append to the shorter array, breaking remaining ties toward arr1.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the n-2 elements triggers a full scan of both arrays.
a.sp: O(n) — storing the two output arrays.

a.n: Approach 2: Coordinate Compression + Two Fenwick Trees (Optimal)
a.i: Compress values to ranks 1..m. Keep a Fenwick tree per array where point-update adds 1 at a value's rank and prefix sums give the count of elements ≤ v; then greaterCount = size − countLE(v). Each operation costs O(log m), so the entire simulation runs in O(n log n), comfortably fitting the constraints even in Python.
s: Sort unique values of nums and map each element to its rank.
Create two empty Fenwick trees t1, t2; insert nums[0] into t1 and nums[1] into t2; set sizes s1=1, s2=1.
For each next element with rank r: c1 = s1 − t1.prefix(r), c2 = s2 − t2.prefix(r) (counts strictly greater).
Choose target by the rules: larger count wins; tie → smaller size wins; still tied → arr1. Update that tree and size.
Concatenate arr1 and arr2 (tracked separately as plain lists) and return.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting/compression is O(n log n) and each of the n operations does O(log n) BIT work.
a.sp: O(n) — the trees, rank map, and output arrays are all linear.

a.n: Approach 3: Sorted Containers / Balanced BST via bisect (Python-friendly alternative)
a.i: Instead of a BIT, keep each array's multiset in a sorted structure (e.g., Python's sortedcontainers.SortedList, or a hand-rolled merge-insertion list). greaterCount(v) = length − index of first element ≥ v via binary search. Insertion cost is O(size) for a plain list due to shifting, giving O(n^2) worst case, but with tiny constants; using SortedList gives true O(n log n). This shows the same idea without writing a BIT.
s: Put nums[0] into sorted list A, nums[1] into sorted list B.
For each new x, find idxA = bisect_left(A, x); count greater = len(A) − idxA; same for B.
Apply the comparison/tie rules to pick A or B.
Insert x at the found position (insort) in the chosen list.
a.t: O(n log n) query time with a balanced structure (SortedList) or O(n^2) worst-case insertion shifts with plain lists — still fast in practice due to memmove-style shifting.
a.sp: O(n) — the sorted copies of both arrays.

w: In an interview, state the brute force first to show you understand the simulation, then immediately note the bottleneck is greaterCount and pivot to the BIT solution — that is the expected answer. Key pitfalls: (1) strictly greater means subtracting the count of elements ≤ v, so use prefix up to the value's own rank (bisect_right / upper_bound semantics); (2) tie-breaking order matters — compare counts first, then lengths, then default to arr1; (3) remember the first two elements are forced into arr1 and arr2 regardless of values. Edge cases include all-equal arrays (Example 3) and strictly decreasing inputs. Likely follow-ups: handle streaming input (BIT handles it naturally), support removals (BIT supports negative updates), or answer offline with a single merged BIT keyed by (arrayId, rank).
